scripts.text:
A sudden spike in traffic

can take an API down for every one of its users.

Let's look at how Stripe keeps its API available with four kinds of limiters.

Adding capacity works the first few times,

but it won't stop one bad actor.

Rate limiting helps when one user spikes, when a runaway or hostile script floods us,

when low-priority requests crowd out critical ones,

and when something breaks inside our own system.

A rate limiter works per user, and fits whenever clients can spread their requests out.

The first and most important caps each user at N requests per second,

with brief bursts for spikes like a flash sale.

Past the limit, the next request is answered with a 429.

The second caps how many requests a user has in progress at once, say twenty,

so retries can't pile onto expensive endpoints.

During incidents we need a load shedder,

which decides on the state of the whole system rather than on who is asking.

The fleet usage shedder reserves a slice of capacity, say 20%, for critical requests

and answers extra non-critical traffic with a 503.

The worker shedder is the last line of defense:

when workers back up,

it slowly sheds test mode traffic first.

Under the hood, Stripe uses the token bucket algorithm.

Every user gets a bucket; each request takes a token,

and fresh tokens drip back in slowly.

If requests come faster than the drip, the bucket runs empty.

If the bucket is empty, the request is rejected.

The buckets live centrally, in Redis.

A limiter must never become the outage. Hook it in so it fails open if its own code or Redis breaks, and return clear, actionable 429 or 503 errors. Keep kill switches and metrics at hand, and dark launch each limiter to see what it would block before it blocks anything.
So start with a request rate limiter, add the other three as you grow, and launch each one carefully.

route.reason: The deliverable is a narrated, multi-scene technical explainer of an article, about two minutes long, with delivery (voice, presenter) decided per scene inside the product. It is not a deck, footage overlay, music piece or short motion unit, and per-scene delivery puts it outside faceless-explainer, so the owning workflow is general-video, which the product wraps.

units.explain: A sudden traffic spike can degrade or take down an API for every user. Adding capacity works at first, but it cannot stop one bad actor, accidental or deliberate, from hurting availability.
preserve: Keep the outage for all users as the stakes, as the source states it
units.question: Why does an API need protecting from traffic at all?

conditions.text: The outage affects all users, not only the one causing the spike.
Stripe operates four kinds of limiters in production.

communicationNeeds.why: The whole video answers this threat; without it the limiters have no purpose
communicationNeeds.need: Let the viewer feel that one user's surge reaches every other user

communicationNeeds.why: It sets up limiting as a different kind of fix, not a bigger server
communicationNeeds.need: Make clear why more capacity alone is not the answer

communicationNeeds.why: The creator's opening frames the video around them
communicationNeeds.need: Promise four kinds of limiters so the viewer can track the tour

units.explain: Four situations: one user spikes; a runaway or hostile script floods the API; low-priority requests crowd out critical ones; something breaks internally and low-priority traffic must be dropped.
units.question: When does rate limiting help?

conditions.text: The four scenarios are one user's spike, a misbehaving or malicious script, low-priority traffic crowding critical traffic, and an internal failure.

communicationNeeds.why: They are the map the limiters later answer; the viewer needs to hold them
communicationNeeds.need: Present the four situations as distinct, recognisable cases

communicationNeeds.why: It foreshadows the split between per-user limiters and system-wide load shedders
communicationNeeds.need: Separate the three caused by users from the one caused inside the system

units.explain: A rate limiter works per user and fits whenever clients can spread their requests out. A load shedder is for incidents: it decides on the state of the whole system, not on who is asking, and drops low-priority requests so critical ones get through.
units.question: What is the difference between a rate limiter and a load shedder?

conditions.text: A rate limiter is appropriate only when clients can change their pace without affecting the outcome.
A load shedder's decision depends on the system's state, not on the requesting user.

communicationNeeds.why: This is the axis that sorts all four limiters into two families
communicationNeeds.need: Show what each kind of limiter looks at when it decides: the user versus the whole system

communicationNeeds.why: It explains why both families exist
communicationNeeds.need: Say that rate limiters are day-to-day tools and load shedders are for emergencies

units.explain: It caps each user at N requests per second, allowing brief bursts above the cap for spikes like a flash sale. Past the limit, the next request is rejected with a 429. It is by far the most important of the four.
preserve: Mark any concrete N as illustrative
Keep 429 as the status for this limiter, as the creator states
units.question: How does the request rate limiter protect the API?

conditions.text: The cap is per user, N requests per second; the source does not give N.
Brief bursts above the cap are allowed for sudden spikes.
A request past the limit is answered with HTTP 429.
Any concrete value shown for N is invented.

communicationNeeds.why: The viewer should see why that particular request gets a 429
communicationNeeds.need: Make the cap perceptible as a per-user rate, and the request that crosses it

communicationNeeds.why: Otherwise the burst allowance reads as the limiter failing
communicationNeeds.need: Distinguish a brief allowed burst from sustained excess

communicationNeeds.why: The closing recommendation depends on it
communicationNeeds.need: Say that this limiter is the most important one

units.explain: Some endpoints are expensive. Users who wait, give up and retry add more demand to an already overloaded resource. Capping the requests a user has in progress at once (the source's example is 20) stops retries from piling on.
preserve: Keep 20 as the source's example, not a recommendation
units.question: Why limit requests in progress rather than requests per second?

conditions.text: The source's example cap is 20 requests in progress at the same time.
Retries against a slow endpoint increase load on it.

communicationNeeds.why: The two per-user limiters differ only on this axis
communicationNeeds.need: Show the contrast between a rate over time and a count of requests in flight at once

communicationNeeds.why: That loop is the reason this limiter exists
communicationNeeds.need: Make the retry feedback loop understandable: slower endpoint, more retries, even slower

units.explain: Traffic is split into critical requests (for example, creating charges) and non-critical ones (for example, listing charges). A fraction of the fleet, 20% in the source's example, is reserved for critical requests; non-critical requests beyond their 80% allocation are rejected with 503.
preserve: Keep 20% as the source's example reservation
units.question: How does the fleet usage shedder keep critical requests flowing?

conditions.text: The reservation in the source's example is 20%, so non-critical traffic may use 80%.
Excess non-critical requests are rejected with status 503.

communicationNeeds.why: The viewer should see that the rejection happens at the allocation boundary, not at full capacity
communicationNeeds.need: Make the reserved share and the non-critical allocation visible as parts of one whole

communicationNeeds.why: Creating versus listing charges makes the priority split concrete
communicationNeeds.need: Name concrete critical and non-critical examples

units.explain: The worker utilization shedder is the last line of defense. When workers back up, it slowly sheds lower-priority traffic in order, starting with test mode traffic, and brings it back slowly to avoid flapping. Unlike the first three, it limits damage from incidents already happening.
units.question: What happens when workers themselves back up?

conditions.text: Traffic is ranked in four categories: critical methods, POSTs, GETs, test mode traffic.
Shedding starts with test mode traffic and escalates only if needed.
Shedding and restoring happen slowly, or the system flaps.

communicationNeeds.why: The order is what protects critical work
communicationNeeds.need: Convey the shedding order from least to most critical, with test mode first

communicationNeeds.why: The source stresses that fast shedding causes flapping
communicationNeeds.need: Convey that shedding is gradual, not a switch

communicationNeeds.why: It completes the layered picture of four defenses
communicationNeeds.need: Place this shedder as damage control after the three preventative limiters

units.explain: With a token bucket. Every user has a bucket; each request takes a token and fresh tokens drip back in slowly. If requests arrive faster than the drip, the bucket empties, and a request to an empty bucket is rejected. The buckets live centrally, in Redis.
preserve: Mark invented bucket sizes and rates as illustrative
units.question: How is a per-user limit actually enforced?

conditions.text: Each request removes one token from that user's bucket.
Tokens are dripped back in slowly.
A request against an empty bucket is rejected.
Any bucket size, drip rate or request count shown is invented.

communicationNeeds.why: The mechanism is the point: admission is spending a token
communicationNeeds.need: Make the link between one request and one token perceptible

communicationNeeds.why: The viewer should understand why rejection follows, not just see it happen
communicationNeeds.need: Show the before, the draining and the after: arrivals faster than the drip empty the bucket, then a request is rejected

communicationNeeds.why: The bucket is how the request rate limiter is enforced
communicationNeeds.need: Connect the empty bucket to the per-user cap from earlier

communicationNeeds.why: It grounds the algorithm in Stripe's implementation
communicationNeeds.need: Say that the buckets live centrally, in Redis

units.explain: Hook it in so it fails open if its own code or Redis breaks; return clear, actionable 429 or 503 errors; keep kill switches, feature flags and metrics at hand; and dark launch each limiter to see what it would block before it blocks anything.
units.question: How do you add a limiter without it becoming the outage?

conditions.text: Errors in the limiter or Redis must let requests through (fail open).
The status is 429 or 503, whichever is most accurate, with an actionable message.

communicationNeeds.why: It is the least intuitive of the four practices and the one that prevents a self-inflicted outage
communicationNeeds.need: Make "fail open" concrete: when the limiter breaks, traffic still flows

communicationNeeds.why: They are actionable advice the viewer takes away
communicationNeeds.need: Let the four practices read as a short, memorable checklist

communicationNeeds.why: It is how thresholds are tuned without hurting existing users
communicationNeeds.need: Explain dark launch as observing what would be blocked before enforcing

units.explain: Not all four are needed on day one. Start with a request rate limiter, add the other three as you grow, and launch each one carefully.
units.question: Where should I begin?

communicationNeeds.why: It turns the tour into a plan the viewer can follow
communicationNeeds.need: Land one clear first action and the order of the rest

communicationNeeds.why: It closes the promise made at the opening
communicationNeeds.need: Recall the four limiters as the whole set, with the first singled out

purpose.message: Stripe keeps its API available by combining per-user rate limiters with system-wide load shedders, enforcing limits with a token bucket in Redis and launching each limiter safely — and you should start with a request rate limiter.
purpose.audience: Developers and engineers who run a production API and need to keep it available under heavy or abusive traffic

delivery.unresolved: No delivery choices have been made. Voice source, presenter visibility and framing are open for every video scene. The base pages' presenter-chip and panel notes are slide reference only.

entities.name: Your API
entities.role: Serves every user's requests; its availability is what the limiters protect
interactions: can be taken down for all users by a traffic spike
stays up for everyone else when one user is limited

entities.name: API user (client)
entities.role: Sends requests; may spike, run a runaway script, or deliberately flood the API
interactions: is capped by the per-user limiters
can usually spread requests out without harm

entities.name: API request
entities.role: The unit of traffic, either critical or non-critical, live or test mode
interactions: is admitted, answered with 429, or shed with 503

entities.name: Request rate limiter
entities.role: Caps each user at N requests per second, with brief bursts allowed
interactions: rejects a user's request past the cap

entities.name: Concurrent requests limiter
entities.role: Caps how many requests a user has in progress at the same time
interactions: stops retries piling onto expensive endpoints

entities.name: Fleet usage load shedder
entities.role: Reserves a fraction of the fleet for critical requests
interactions: rejects non-critical requests over their allocation with 503

entities.name: Worker utilization load shedder
entities.role: Final line of defense that sheds lower-priority traffic when workers back up
interactions: sheds test mode traffic first, then escalates slowly

entities.name: Workers
entities.role: Respond to incoming requests in parallel; their spare capacity is tracked
interactions: back up under load, triggering the worker shedder

entities.name: Token bucket
entities.role: Per-user store of request allowance: each request takes a token, tokens drip back slowly
interactions: admits a request while it holds a token

entities.name: Redis
entities.role: The central store where the buckets and counters live
interactions: if it goes down, the limiter must fail open

uncertainty.text: The source calls all four "rate limiters" (¶47) while also separating load shedders from rate limiters (¶12–¶13). The creator's scripts use "limiters" for all four and "rate limiter" / "load shedder" for the two families; the video should keep one usage.

The source does not state outright that the request rate limiter answers with 429; it implies 429 for rate limiting (¶26) and asks implementers to choose between 429 and 503 (¶52). The creator's script states 429.
The source does not give a value for N or for the bucket's size or drip rate; any value shown must be marked illustrative.

creativeGuidance.text: The creator gave no direction for the video; the scene scripts are drafts under the draft wording policy and may be revised.
Keep one visual identity for each limiter and for the request across the whole video, so the four limiters read as layers of one system rather than four separate topics.
Use the theme's accent only for what the viewer must look at now, such as the request being rejected or the token being taken.
Treat the two per-user limiters and the two load shedders as two families, so the difference in what each one looks at stays visible.
